subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Biology Cells Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on cells, diffusion, microscopy and practical skills.
description: A KS3 science reading pack based on the supplied cells study material. The passages test comprehension, inference, explanation and practical reasoning about cell structure, specialised cells, diffusion, microscopy and magnification.

data.sourcePassage: Cells are the smallest living units of organisms. Every living thing is made of one or more cells, and cells carry out life processes such as respiration, growth, repair and responding to their surroundings. Some organisms are unicellular, which means they are made of one cell. Amoeba, yeast and bacteria are examples. Other organisms are multicellular, which means they are made of many cells. In a multicellular organism, similar cells work together as tissues. Different tissues work together as organs, and organs work together in organ systems. The whole living thing is the organism. For example, a muscle cell can be part of muscle tissue, muscle tissue can form part of the heart, and the heart works in the circulatory system of a human.

questions.question: What is a cell?
questions.modelAnswer: A cell is the smallest living unit of an organism.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct order from smallest to largest?
options: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
organism, organ system, organ, tissue, cell
cell, organ, tissue, organism, organ system
tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system
questions.modelAnswer: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism

questions.question: Explain the difference between unicellular and multicellular organisms.
questions.modelAnswer: Unicellular organisms are made of one cell, while multicellular organisms are made of many cells.

questions.question: Why do multicellular organisms need levels of organisation?
questions.modelAnswer: Many specialised cells need to work together, so cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs form organ systems that carry out life processes.

questions.question: Use the passage to give a human example of cell organisation.
questions.modelAnswer: A muscle cell is part of muscle tissue, which can form part of the heart, and the heart works in the circulatory system of a human.

data.sourcePassage: Plant and animal cells share several important structures. Both usually have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. The nucleus controls many cell activities and contains genetic information. The cytoplasm is where many chemical reactions happen. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell. Mitochondria are where most aerobic respiration happens, and ribosomes make proteins. Plant cells also have structures that animal cells do not have. A cellulose cell wall supports and strengthens the cell. A permanent vacuole contains cell sap and helps keep the cell firm. Many green plant cells have chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll and absorb light for photosynthesis. However, not every plant cell has chloroplasts. Root hair cells are underground, so they usually do not receive light and usually do not contain chloroplasts.

questions.question: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
options: Cell membrane
Cell wall
Ribosome
Permanent vacuole
questions.modelAnswer: Cell membrane

questions.question: Name two structures found in both plant and animal cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say that all plant cells contain chloroplasts?
questions.modelAnswer: Some plant cells, such as root hair cells, are underground and do not receive light, so they usually do not contain chloroplasts.

questions.question: A cell has a cell wall, a large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts. What type of cell is it likely to be, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: It is likely to be a plant cell because those structures are found in plant cells but not animal cells.

questions.question: Explain why the cell wall and cell membrane should not be confused.
questions.modelAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid cellulose layer that supports plant cells, while the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

data.sourceTitle: How Specialised Cells Fit Their Jobs
data.targetTitle: How Specialised Cells Fit Their Jobs
data.sourcePassage: A specialised cell has adaptations that help it carry out a particular job. Good explanations link the structure of the cell to its function. A red blood cell carries oxygen in the blood. Its biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area for oxygen exchange, it contains haemoglobin to carry oxygen, and it has no nucleus when mature so there is more space for haemoglobin. A root hair cell absorbs water and mineral ions from soil. Its long hair-like projection increases surface area for absorption. A sperm cell has a tail to swim towards an egg cell and many mitochondria to release energy for movement. A palisade cell is found near the top of leaves and contains many chloroplasts so it can absorb light for photosynthesis.

questions.question: What is a specialised cell?
questions.modelAnswer: A specialised cell is a cell with adaptations that help it carry out a particular job.

questions.question: Which adaptation helps a root hair cell absorb water and mineral ions?
options: A long hair-like projection
A tail
A biconcave disc shape
Cilia
questions.modelAnswer: A long hair-like projection

questions.question: Explain how a mature red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen.
questions.modelAnswer: It has a biconcave disc shape for a large surface area, contains haemoglobin to carry oxygen and has no nucleus when mature to give more space for haemoglobin.

questions.question: Why does a sperm cell need many mitochondria?
questions.modelAnswer: It needs many mitochondria to release energy for movement, so it can swim towards an egg cell.

questions.question: Write a structure-function explanation for a palisade cell.
questions.modelAnswer: A palisade cell contains many chloroplasts, which increases light absorption, so it can carry out photosynthesis effectively.

data.sourceTitle: Diffusion Into And Out Of Cells
data.targetTitle: Diffusion Into And Out Of Cells
data.sourcePassage: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. Particles in liquids and gases move randomly, so they do not choose where to go. Over time, more particles move from the high concentration region to the low concentration region than in the opposite direction. Diffusion can happen in living and non-living systems. In organisms, small particles such as oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse across cell membranes. Oxygen diffuses from air sacs in the lungs into the blood because oxygen concentration is higher in the air sacs than in the blood entering the lungs. Carbon dioxide diffuses out of respiring cells into the blood because carbon dioxide concentration is higher in the cells. A bigger concentration difference, a higher temperature, a larger surface area and a shorter diffusion distance can increase the rate of diffusion.

questions.question: What is diffusion?
options: Net movement from higher concentration to lower concentration
Net movement from lower concentration to higher concentration
Particles choosing to move where they are needed
Movement that only happens in living cells
questions.modelAnswer: Net movement from higher concentration to lower concentration

questions.question: Name two gases that can diffuse across cell membranes.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse across cell membranes.

questions.question: Why does oxygen diffuse from air sacs in the lungs into the blood?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen concentration is higher in the air sacs than in the blood entering the lungs, so oxygen diffuses down the concentration gradient into the blood.

questions.question: Explain why higher temperature can make diffusion faster.
questions.modelAnswer: At a higher temperature, particles usually move faster, so they spread out more quickly.

questions.question: A student says diffusion only happens in living things. Use the passage to correct this misconception.
questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion happens in living and non-living systems because particles in liquids and gases move randomly. Food colouring spreading in water is a non-living example.

data.sourcePassage: Light microscopes are used to see cells that are too small to view clearly with the naked eye. To use a microscope safely, students should start with the lowest power objective lens, place the slide on the stage, secure it with clips, adjust the light source, use the coarse focus knob to bring the specimen into view and then use the fine focus knob to sharpen the image. Higher magnification does not always mean a better image because the image may be harder to focus or may have poor resolution. Total microscope magnification is calculated by multiplying eyepiece magnification by objective magnification. Magnification can also be calculated using image size divided by actual size. In practical work, students should identify variables, keep control variables the same, repeat measurements, calculate means and evaluate limitations. Agar cubes are useful models for diffusion, but they are not living cells and do not have real organelles.

questions.question: Which objective lens should students use first when using a microscope?
questions.modelAnswer: Students should start with the lowest power objective lens.

questions.question: How is total microscope magnification calculated?
options: Eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification
Image size multiplied by actual size
Actual size divided by image size
Objective magnification minus eyepiece magnification
questions.modelAnswer: Eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification

questions.question: Why does higher magnification not always mean a better image?
questions.modelAnswer: At higher magnification the image can be harder to focus and may have poor resolution, so it may be blurry or unclear.

questions.question: Why should students repeat measurements in a diffusion investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeats improve reliability because anomalies can be spotted and a mean can be calculated.

questions.question: Give one limitation of using agar cubes as model cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Agar cubes are not living cells and do not have real cell membranes, cytoplasm or organelles.
